paragraphs: Apprenticeship learning asks how to act well from expert demonstrations when the true reward function is unknown. A common strategy treats imitation as classification: learn to predict the action the expert would take. This paper gives a formal analysis of how errors in those predictions translate into differences between the apprentice’s policy value and the expert’s.

The main result connects a classifier’s error rate, epsilon, to a policy-value gap of order square root of epsilon. When the expert’s policy is close to optimal, the paper proves the stronger bound of order epsilon. Thus, the quality of the expert changes the relationship between action-prediction accuracy and overall performance, rather than merely changing the behavior being copied.

The stronger result also has a consequence for collecting demonstrations. Successfully imitating a near-optimal expert can require far fewer examples, according to the analysis. This suggests potential savings when expert demonstrations are costly or difficult to obtain and the expert is known to perform well.
neurips-2010-a-reduction-from-apprentice.tldr: The paper bounds imitation’s performance gap and shows that a near-optimal expert can make successful learning require fewer demonstrations.

paragraphs: Boosting builds an accurate predictor by combining classifiers that are individually weak. For two-class problems, the theoretical relationship between weak learners and boosting is well understood. This paper addresses the corresponding multiclass problem, where predictions must distinguish among more than two categories and the appropriate requirements on a weak learner had been less clearly established.

The authors introduce a broad framework that makes those requirements precise. Within it, they identify optimal conditions on the weak classifier and construct boosting algorithms that operate under those conditions. The contribution therefore links two questions: what the component learner must provide, and how a boosting procedure should use that capability.

This matters because claims about the effectiveness of a boosting algorithm depend on the assumptions made about its weak learner. The framework supplies a common basis for expressing both. Its optimality claims are made within that framework and in the particular sense studied by the paper; the abstract does not claim that one algorithm is universally best for every multiclass application.
neurips-2010-a-theory-of-multiclass-boos.tldr: A general multiclass boosting framework identifies optimal weak-learner requirements and designs algorithms that are most effective in the framework’s stated sense.

paragraphs: Active learning chooses which unlabeled examples should receive labels. Two common priorities are informativeness, meaning how useful a label could be for learning, and representativeness, meaning how well an example reflects the available data. The paper addresses how to bring these priorities together through a systematic selection rule.

The proposed method, QUIRE, uses a min-max formulation of active learning. That formulation provides a principled basis for measuring and combining informativeness and representativeness. Its central contribution is the joint treatment of the two criteria: the choice of an example is guided by a shared framework instead of an ad hoc combination of separate preferences.

The authors report extensive experiments in which QUIRE outperforms several leading active learning methods. These results support the practical value of its selection framework on the evaluated problems. The finding is empirical: it shows that the proposed combination can improve query selection in those comparisons, rather than establishing that QUIRE will select the best example in every learning setting.
neurips-2010-active-learning-by-querying.tldr: QUIRE systematically combines informativeness and representativeness for active learning and outperforms several leading methods in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Expert demonstrations often cover only a small fraction of the situations an apprentice may encounter. Inverse reinforcement learning can generalize from those demonstrations by assuming that the expert maximizes a utility expressed as a linear combination of state-action features. Learning then depends on estimating the expected accumulated feature counts under the expert’s behavior.

The paper shows that the quality of the resulting policy is highly sensitive to errors in those estimates. Many inverse reinforcement learning methods use straightforward Monte Carlo estimates from demonstrations. The authors propose bootstrapping the demonstrations to reduce estimation error, drawing on two explicit assumptions: the expert is optimal or nearly optimal, and the system’s dynamics are known.

Experiments on gridworld and car racing problems show that the approach can learn good policies from few demonstrations. The result connects a practical data shortage to a specific estimation problem. Under the stated assumptions, using knowledge about expert quality and system behavior can help extract more useful learning information from limited demonstrations.
neurips-2010-bootstrapping-apprenticeshi.tldr: Bootstrapping expert demonstrations improves feature-count estimation and learns good policies from few examples when expert quality and system dynamics are known.

paragraphs: Causal discovery becomes challenging when relevant information comes from different experiments and must be combined with background knowledge. Methods that combine datasets from identical experiments do not address this broader situation. The paper introduces MCI, an algorithm intended to infer causal relations from models associated with different experiments.

Its foundation is a decomposition of constraint-based causal discovery into two stages: identifying candidate pairs and then eliminating candidates. The authors show that these stages can be applied separately using different models. This creates a way to combine evidence without requiring all the contributing experiments to be identical, while producing an interpretable description of the inferred relationships.

The paper proves validity of the inferred causal relations in the large-sample limit. Tests on varied synthetic collections of input models examine the algorithm’s behavior and output quality. The authors describe the method as fast and reliable, while treating applications to real-world settings, including large databases, as promising directions for adaptation rather than established results of those tests.
neurips-2010-causal-discovery-in-multipl.tldr: MCI combines models from different experiments to infer causal relations with a validity guarantee in the large-sample limit.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation aims to transfer useful information from a source domain to a target domain. This paper introduces EA++, a semi-supervised method that uses unlabeled target examples to support that transfer. It builds on EASYADAPT’s augmented feature-space idea and adds a co-regularization approach for incorporating the target data.

The method is designed to be simple to implement and usable as preprocessing for any supervised learner. Its theoretical analysis compares EA++ with EASYADAPT through Rademacher complexity, a measure used to study the flexibility of a hypothesis class. The authors show that EA++ has a lower-complexity hypothesis class in their analysis, yielding tighter generalization bounds.

Sentiment analysis experiments support the theoretical findings and demonstrate the method’s effectiveness against EASYADAPT and several other baselines. The bounds and experiments offer complementary evidence: the analysis explains a change in the learning class, while the experiments show useful predictive behavior on the evaluated tasks. Together, they support using unlabeled target data within this straightforward adaptation framework.
neurips-2010-co-regularization-based-sem.tldr: EA++ uses unlabeled target data in a simple adaptation procedure with tighter generalization bounds and supporting sentiment analysis results.

paragraphs: Continuous Markov random fields describe joint probability distributions over outcomes that vary continuously. To answer questions about particular outcomes, one often needs marginal distributions, which summarize selected variables while accounting for the others. This paper studies both the computational difficulty of obtaining those marginals and methods for approximating them.

The authors prove that marginal computation for constrained continuous Markov random fields is #P-hard in general. They also give a polynomial-time approximation scheme under assumptions about the field’s structure that they describe as mild. These results distinguish the difficult general problem from structured cases where approximation has a stronger computational guarantee. A sampling algorithm and additional efficiency techniques provide another part of the proposed inference toolkit.

The paper applies continuous Markov random fields to statistical relational learning and evaluates the algorithm on collective classification. In that setting, the standard deviation of marginal distributions proves useful as a confidence measure. The findings therefore concern both computing predictions and extracting useful uncertainty information from the resulting distributions.
neurips-2010-computing-marginal-distribu.tldr: The paper establishes general marginal-inference hardness, develops approximation and sampling methods, and finds marginal spread useful for confidence in collective classification.

paragraphs: Supervised dimensionality reduction seeks a compact representation that helps classification while controlling learning capacity. This paper introduces a forward probabilistic model that extends reduced-rank regression to multinomial outcomes. It also gives a probabilistic interpretation of discriminative clustering, with stated benefits in hyperparameter requirements and optimization.

A central difficulty is that expectation-maximization optimizes a nonconvex objective containing many local minima. The authors introduce a local approximation that produces a quadratic, still nonconvex problem over a product of simplices, or collections of probability vectors. They then develop an efficient optimization algorithm using convex relaxation and a low-rank representation of the data, allowing larger instances to be handled.

Text document classification experiments show the model outperforming other supervised dimensionality reduction methods in the reported comparisons. Separate unsupervised clustering simulations show advantages of the probabilistic formulation over existing discriminative clustering approaches. The contribution combines a model interpretation with an optimization strategy, and the two experimental settings provide evidence for benefits in both supervised representation learning and clustering.
neurips-2010-efficient-optimization-for-.tldr: A probabilistic latent-class model uses local approximation, convex relaxation, and low-rank structure to improve optimization and reported classification and clustering results.

paragraphs: This paper estimates Rényi entropy and mutual information from samples without specifying a parametric distribution. Its starting assumptions are independent, identically distributed observations from an unknown absolutely continuous distribution in a Euclidean space. The aim is to compute useful information quantities directly from the geometry of the observed sample.

The estimators use generalized nearest-neighbor graphs. For entropy, the calculation sums powers of Euclidean edge lengths in a graph built from the sample. For mutual information, it uses the corresponding construction on the sample’s empirical copula, a representation of dependence. The authors describe these estimators as simple and computationally efficient.

The paper proves almost-sure consistency: as sample size grows, the estimates converge to their targets with probability one. It also gives upper bounds on convergence rates under the additional assumption of a Lipschitz-continuous density, which controls how quickly density values can change. Experiments demonstrate usefulness in independent subspace analysis, connecting the theoretical guarantees to a concrete application of information estimation.
neurips-2010-estimation-of-renyi-entropy.tldr: Nearest-neighbor graph estimators of Rényi entropy and mutual information receive consistency proofs and convergence-rate bounds under a density smoothness assumption.

paragraphs: Generalized Binary Search identifies an unknown object by asking yes-or-no questions, with the aim of using few queries. This paper gives the method a coding-theoretic interpretation. Under that view, it constructs a question sequence from the top down, greedily reducing the expected number of queries needed to identify the object.

The interpretation leads to two extensions with different objectives. In the first, objects belong to groups and the learner only needs to identify the correct group. Distinguishing every object is therefore unnecessary. In the second, the cost of identification grows exponentially with the number of questions, making long query sequences more expensive than under a simple query-count objective.

For both settings, the authors derive exact expressions for the objectives using Shannon or Rényi entropy and develop greedy algorithms to minimize them. The exactness applies to the objective formulas; the algorithms are described as greedy. The contribution shows how a coding perspective can adapt question selection to what must be identified and how questions are charged.
neurips-2010-extensions-of-generalized-b.tldr: A coding-theoretic interpretation extends Generalized Binary Search to group identification and exponentially increasing query costs.

paragraphs: Classification data can have missing features during training, testing, or both. This paper changes how an example is represented: it becomes a set of observed feature-value pairs. Missing entries fit naturally into this representation because the example is described by the pairs that are available, rather than by a fully populated fixed-length vector.

The method maps each feature-value pair into an embedding space and then combines the embedded vectors nonlinearly to classify the set. Both the embedding parameters and the combination parameters are learned jointly for the final classification objective. This ties the representation of individual observations to the way their collective information is used for prediction.

The embedding step also offers flexibility for encoding prior knowledge about features. Across several datasets, the authors report advantageous results compared with alternative approaches. The contribution is therefore both representational and predictive: it supplies a way to express incomplete examples and shows that learning directly with this representation can be effective in the tested classification problems.
neurips-2010-feature-set-embedding-for-i.tldr: Representing incomplete examples as sets of observed feature-value pairs enables jointly learned embeddings and classification with favorable reported results.

paragraphs: Gated Softmax Classification models class probabilities through multiplicative interactions between an input vector and binary latent variables. These hidden variables have exponentially many possible joint configurations. The paper’s key computational result is that class probabilities can nevertheless be computed efficiently and exactly by summing out the latent variables.

Exact marginalization also makes the exact log-likelihood gradient available for learning. The model expresses its bilinear scores through a three-dimensional weight tensor. The authors show that factorizing this tensor lets the model learn a dictionary of invariant basis functions, providing a mechanism for encoding invariances inherent in the classification task.

Experiments on benchmark problems find classification performance competitive with kernel support vector machines, backpropagation, and deep belief networks. The stated result is competitiveness, rather than uniform superiority. The broader contribution combines expressive latent interactions with tractable probabilistic calculations: the model can account for many hidden configurations while retaining exact class probabilities and exact learning gradients, and its factorization offers a way to represent task-related invariance.
neurips-2010-gated-softmax-classificatio.tldr: A gated probabilistic classifier supports efficient exact latent-variable marginalization and uses tensor factorization to learn task invariances.

paragraphs: Preference elicitation learns what a user values by asking questions about their preferences. Bayesian approaches represent uncertainty about the user’s hidden utility function. This paper addresses how preferences collected from earlier users can help with a new user, with the aim of reducing the amount of questioning that newcomer needs.

The authors place a Gaussian process prior over utility functions defined jointly through user and item features. They learn its hyperparameters from previous users’ preferences and use the resulting model during elicitation for a new user. This gives a flexible shared utility model that can carry information across users while retaining uncertainty about their preferences.

The approach supports an efficient value-of-information heuristic for choosing questions and a principled way to feed newly elicited preferences back into the shared model. Comparisons with previous work on a real dataset of sushi preferences demonstrate its effectiveness. The result supports combining knowledge transfer and query selection within a single probabilistic preference model, rather than treating each new elicitation session independently.
neurips-2010-gaussian-process-preference.tldr: A Gaussian process preference model transfers information from previous users and supports value-of-information query selection for new users.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to retrieve database points close to a query hyperplane without scanning the entire database. This differs from searching near a single query point: the desired results lie near a boundary. The authors develop two hashing approaches that retrieve nearby points in sublinear time.

The first approach assigns two-bit keys that are locality-sensitive to the angle between a database point and the hyperplane’s normal. The second embeds the data in a space where a Euclidean norm represents the desired point-to-hyperplane distance. The methods have a stated tradeoff: the first needs more efficient preprocessing, while the second offers stronger accuracy guarantees.

For pool-based active learning, the current hyperplane classifier becomes the query. The retrieval procedures approximately select examples meeting the minimum-distance-to-hyperplane criterion. Experiments demonstrate the tradeoffs between the two approaches and show that active selection becomes practical with millions of unlabeled examples. The contribution makes this established selection criterion more computationally accessible at large scale.
neurips-2010-hashing-hyperplane-queries-.tldr: Two hashing methods approximately retrieve points near a classifier’s hyperplane, making active selection practical over millions of unlabeled examples.

paragraphs: Human ratings can depend on recent experience rather than a stable, absolute scale. This paper treats those sequential effects as systematic influences that can be modeled, instead of merely unpredictable noise. Its goal is to recover more meaningful judgments from a sequence whose individual ratings have been shaped by earlier experiences.

The authors formulate this correction as inference over latent internal states, such as sensations that are not directly observed. Relative judgment introduces temporal dependencies into that inference problem. Their proposed solution uses a conditional random field with constraints motivated by psychological theories, connecting the computational model to an account of how people produce ratings.

Two experiments on a simple length-estimation task supply ground-truth rating data for examining the models. The decontamination techniques reduce human judgment error by more than 20% in the reported work. This supports the possibility of correcting systematic sequential influences in that setting; surveys and questionnaires provide the broader motivation, while the stated experimental evidence comes from length estimation.
neurips-2010-improving-human-judgments-b.tldr: A psychologically constrained conditional random field corrects sequential effects in ratings, reducing judgment error by over 20% in length-estimation experiments.

paragraphs: Importance weighting adjusts the contributions of training examples when training and test distributions differ. This paper examines its behavior with finite samples, beginning with simple cases in which the technique can fail. The aim is to identify conditions that support generalization guarantees and use that analysis to inform a learning procedure.

The authors establish upper and lower generalization bounds when weights are bounded. They also provide guarantees for unbounded weights under the weaker requirement that their second moment is finite. That condition is related to Rényi divergence between the training and test distributions, connecting the guarantees to how those distributions differ.

The analysis develops general bounds for unbounded loss functions, which also have relevance beyond importance weighting. These bounds guide an alternative reweighting algorithm, and experiments demonstrate benefits of that algorithm. The paper additionally analyzes normalized importance weights. Together, the results explain why reweighting requires care with finite data and extend the theoretical treatment beyond the restrictive case of uniformly bounded weights.
neurips-2010-learning-bounds-for-importa.tldr: The paper gives finite-sample importance-weighting guarantees, including for unbounded weights with finite second moments, and derives an alternative reweighting algorithm.

paragraphs: Learning several parametric models together can be viewed as estimating a matrix, with tasks along one dimension and features along the other. This paper introduces a matrix-normal penalty that couples those models. Its purpose is to represent relationships among tasks alongside structure in the features used to predict them.

The penalty decomposes the full covariance of the parameter matrix into a Kronecker product of task and feature covariances. To address overfitting and select meaningful relationships, the authors impose L1 penalties on both inverse covariance matrices. This encourages sparse structures in the relationships being learned. Several existing methods appear as variants of special cases within the formulation.

Experiments examine landmine detection across multiple fields and face recognition across different subjects, comparing the approach with related models. The reported findings support its effectiveness and flexibility for representing different task structures. The contribution is a joint framework in which task relatedness and feature representation are both learned under regularization, rather than leaving either type of structure outside the model.
neurips-2010-learning-multiple-tasks-wit.tldr: A matrix-normal penalty with sparse task and feature inverse covariances jointly models relationships across multiple learning tasks.

paragraphs: Structured sparsity encourages a learning model to select variables according to groups or relationships. This paper considers a penalty formed by summing the infinity norms of variable groups. Its focus is general overlapping groups, a setting beyond the disjoint or specially hierarchical group structures emphasized by many earlier optimization methods.

The authors show that the penalty’s proximal problem is dual to a quadratic minimum-cost flow problem. A proximal problem is an optimization step that combines a penalty with a preference for staying near a given point. The flow connection enables an efficient procedure that solves this step exactly in polynomial time, providing a computational tool for learning with the specified penalty.

The algorithm scales to millions of groups and variables. Experiments using image and video data demonstrate applicability and scalability across several problems. The significance is that general overlap becomes computationally manageable for this family of penalties, expanding the structures that sparse models can use without restricting groups to a simple hierarchy.
neurips-2010-network-flow-algorithms-for.tldr: A network-flow formulation solves a structured-sparsity proximal problem exactly in polynomial time, supporting general overlapping groups at large scale.

paragraphs: Bayesian preference elicitation often chooses questions by their expected value of information: how useful the answer is expected to be for the next decision. Computing the best question under this myopic criterion can be expensive. This paper studies choice queries, where a user selects their preferred product from a presented set.

Under very general assumptions, the authors show that the optimal choice-query set also maximizes the expected utility of the user’s selection as a recommendation set. This equivalence turns query selection into a simpler submodular optimization problem. It can substantially reduce the computational burden of both exact methods and greedy approximation methods.

The paper also considers erroneous user responses under two specified noise models and provides worst-case guarantees. A local search method is presented for large outcome spaces and reported to work well. The central insight is a conditional equivalence between asking an informative choice question and offering a valuable set of options, which makes the myopic query-selection problem easier to compute.
neurips-2010-optimal-bayesian-recommenda.tldr: Under general assumptions, optimal recommendation sets are also myopically optimal choice queries, enabling simpler information-value optimization.

paragraphs: This paper develops a fast online solver for large maximum-flow problems and applies it to arranging web pages across cache tiers. The application asks how to place pages in a layered caching system to serve an incoming query stream optimally. The computational method produces approximate solutions to the underlying flow problem.

The authors start from an integer linear program and exploit total unimodularity, a structural property of its constraint matrix. Together with Lagrangian relaxation, this allows the problem to be handled as a convex online game. The algorithm then uses stochastic gradient descent over a set of flows to generate approximate maximum-flow solutions.

The caching application involves more than 80 million web pages, and experiments on real query-page data demonstrate the method’s effectiveness. The result shows the solver being used at substantial scale for a concrete allocation problem. The paper also identifies maximum-flow applications in portfolio optimization, inventory management, computer vision, and logistics, while its stated empirical demonstration concerns web-page tiering.
neurips-2010-optimal-web-scale-tiering-a.tldr: An online approximate maximum-flow solver optimizes cache-tier placement for over 80 million web pages using stochastic gradient descent.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning uses data with incomplete label information. This paper studies a setting where the missingness can be partial and arbitrary, rather than random. That matters because the labels that remain available may reflect an unfavorable selection process, changing what a learner can infer from the observed information.

Under assumptions about the label information that is available, the authors derive nearly matching upper and lower generalization bounds. The upper bounds describe achievable learning guarantees, while the lower bounds constrain what can be achieved in the setting. Their close agreement gives a relatively sharp theoretical picture under the stated assumptions.

The analysis motivates a convex optimization formulation for estimating model parameters. The authors develop an efficient algorithm and analyze its convergence. Experiments on several standard datasets show robustness to missing-label patterns and performance exceeding several strong baselines. The contribution connects a more demanding model of missing information with both theoretical guarantees and an algorithm whose reported empirical behavior supports that motivation.
neurips-2010-semi-supervised-learning-wi.tldr: The paper analyzes arbitrary missing-label patterns and develops a convex learning method with theoretical guarantees and empirical robustness.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes express dependencies between random variables through a covariance structure. In Bayesian models, hyperparameters governing that structure can themselves be uncertain. Integrating over them lets predictions account for multiple possible explanations of the data, rather than relying on one fixed covariance setting.

Markov chain Monte Carlo is often used to perform that integration. With non-Gaussian observations, however, standard hyperparameter sampling methods can require careful tuning and may converge slowly. This paper introduces a slice sampling approach intended to make exploration of the covariance hyperparameters more effective with little manual tuning.

The authors report that the method mixes well in both strong-data and weak-data regimes. Mixing describes how effectively the sampling process moves through the possibilities it must explore, so this property matters for representing hyperparameter uncertainty through samples. The contribution addresses the computational step needed to average over covariance explanations, with the stated advantage extending across regimes where the observations provide different amounts of information.
neurips-2010-slice-sampling-covariance-h.tldr: A slice sampler explores latent Gaussian model covariance hyperparameters with little tuning and good mixing in strong- and weak-data regimes.

paragraphs: Sparse supervised learning seeks useful linear predictors that rely on few variables. The usual selection cost counts the chosen variables, and its convex relaxation leads to the L1 norm. This paper generalizes that idea by allowing the cost of a selected set to express prior knowledge or structural preferences.

For nondecreasing submodular set functions, the authors show how to obtain the corresponding convex envelope through the Lovász extension. This produces a family of polyhedral norms. They provide computational tools, including subgradients and proximal operators, along with theoretical conditions for recovering the selected-variable support and for inference in high-dimensional settings.

Choosing different submodular functions gives new interpretations of known penalties, including rank-based norms and group norms with overlapping groups. The framework also yields new norms that can encode priors involving dependencies among variables. Its significance is a systematic connection between a structured preference over variable sets and a convex penalty that can be optimized, with guarantees stated through the conditions developed in the paper.
neurips-2010-structured-sparsity-inducin.tldr: Submodular set functions yield structured sparsity norms through convex envelopes, unifying existing penalties and enabling new ones.

paragraphs: Kernel methods can operate on inputs such as probability measures, trees, and graphs, beyond ordinary finite-dimensional vectors. Yet their successful use does not by itself supply the function-space properties needed for known consistency results. This paper addresses the construction of universal kernels for certain nonstandard input spaces.

The authors develop a general technique based on Taylor-type kernels that explicitly constructs universal kernels on compact metric spaces outside the usual Euclidean setting. Universality supplies a sufficiently rich function space for approximation and is one route to the consistency guarantees discussed for support vector machines. Compactness is part of the stated construction setting.

The paper applies the technique to spaces of probability measures, kernels based on Fourier transforms, and signal-processing kernels. These constructions address the gap between theoretically useful assumptions and kernels of practical interest for nonstandard inputs. The contribution is therefore a method for building kernels with the desired theoretical property, rather than an empirical comparison of prediction accuracy across applications.
neurips-2010-universal-kernels-on-non-st.tldr: A Taylor-type construction produces universal kernels on compact nonstandard metric spaces, including spaces of probability measures.

paragraphs: Linear discriminant analysis reduces dimensionality using measures of variation within classes and separation between classes. This paper analyzes those scatter measures and characterizes the conventional formulation as taking an average-case view. It proposes worst-case linear discriminant analysis, or WLDA, using newly defined within-class and between-class measures.

The authors argue that this worst-case perspective can be more suitable for classification. They offer two optimization approaches depending on problem size. When the number of examples or features is not very large, they relax the problem into a metric-learning formulation. For larger settings, a greedy method constructs the transformation one direction at a time.

The paper also analyzes a special case to clarify the relationship between WLDA and conventional LDA. Experiments on several benchmark datasets demonstrate effectiveness against related dimensionality reduction methods. These findings support the proposed perspective in the evaluated settings, while the claim that worst-case scatter is more suitable for classification remains a motivation rather than a universal conclusion.
neurips-2010-worst-case-linear-discrimin.tldr: WLDA replaces average-case scatter measures with a worst-case formulation and shows effective dimensionality reduction in benchmark comparisons.
